Use the **Explore** subagent. It's built for "Where is X?" and "How does Y work?" questions: it does a fast, read-only search of your codebase and runs off your main context, so it won't clutter your conversation.

The other options don't fit as well. The **Build** agent has full read-and-write power, which you don't need for a lookup. **Plan** mode is meant for scoping large or risky changes.

Run:

```bash
100xprompt auth list
```

This shows which credentials are currently active. To add another credential, run `100xprompt auth login` again.

Run:

```
100xprompt models
```

This lists every model you can select right now, along with the exact identifiers to use in your config (for example, `100xprompt/pro` in `100xprompt.json`).

Use **Plan (read-only)** mode. It's built for exactly this: exploring a codebase or having 100xprompt draft a plan before it touches anything.

In Plan mode, 100xprompt can read, search, and propose a full plan. Every state-changing action is blocked, including file edits, commands, and spawning sub-agents. The docs call it the safest way to start on an unfamiliar codebase, because the AI is physically unable to change anything.

To turn it on, use the **Cycle permission mode** command in the terminal app, or set the mode explicitly. It applies for the rest of the session and doesn't rewrite your saved config.

Once you're happy with the plan, switch to:
- **Default** to have sensitive actions ask for approval, or
- **Accept edits** to have file changes auto-approved while commands still ask.
The default shortcut is `<leader>t`: press your leader key (`ctrl+x` by default), then `t`. This triggers the **theme list** action, which opens the theme picker.

You can create a **share link**, which is a URL that opens your session in the browser so others can view it. There are two ways to create one:

- **Use the share action** from within your session.
- **Use the `--share` flag.**

To change what happens by default, use the `share` setting.

A session includes the full conversation along with its history, context, and results. For more details, see [Sharing](/enterprise/sharing).

Switch to the **Pro** model, which is built for deep reasoning, large refactors, and hard problems.

In the terminal interface:

1. Run the `/models` command.
2. Select **Pro**. You can switch between **Flash** and **Pro** at any time.

You can also use the variant option to set the reasoning effort.

Pass the agent's name with the `--agent` flag when you start the run:

```bash
100xprompt run --agent plan "map out how billing is wired up"
```

To use a different agent, put its name in place of `plan` (for example, `build`).

Your choice of agent controls what the run is allowed to do:
- **Plan** is read-only. It can look at your code but won't change it.
- **Build** has full read and write access, so it can make edits and run commands.

To run the server without a browser window opening, use `serve` instead of `web`:

```bash
100xprompt serve
```

This starts a headless server. (`100xprompt web` is the command that starts the server and also opens the app in your default browser.)

To connect to it:

1. **Open the web app** in any browser.
2. **Check the server URL.** The connect screen fills in the address of the server you launched, for example `http://localhost:4096`. Keep it if the server is on the same machine. To connect remotely, change it to the other machine's address.
3. **Enter an API key if needed.** If the server is protected with an API key, put it in the **API Key** field. For a local, unprotected server, leave the field blank.
4. **Select Connect.** The app checks that the server is reachable, then opens your workspace.

If you expose the web app beyond your own machine, protect it with an API key so only trusted people can connect.

Subject: Re: Agent paused before running a system command

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out, and sorry for the confusion. What you saw is most likely 100xprompt working as designed rather than an error.

**Why it paused**

100xprompt asks for your approval before it does anything sensitive, and running a system command is that kind of action. So instead of executing the command on its own, the agent stopped and waited for your go-ahead. This keeps you in control of what happens on your machine and in your project, and every change it makes stays yours to review, refine, or roll back.

**What to do next**

1. **Go back to your session and look at the pending request.** Check which command the agent wants to run and whether it makes sense for your task.
2. **Approve it or decline it.** If the command looks right, approve it and the agent will continue working toward finishing the task. If it doesn't, decline it and tell the agent how you'd like it to proceed instead.
3. **Review the results.** Once the task is done, you can review any changes it made and refine or roll them back as needed.

If you'd like to change how often 100xprompt asks before acting, see the **Configuration** section of our docs, which covers settings and permissions.

If the agent didn't show any approval request, or it stayed stuck after you responded, please reply with which surface you were using (terminal, web, or IDE) and a short description of what you saw. We'll look into it.

Best regards,
100xprompt Support

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out. Nothing is broken; this is expected behavior.

**What's happening**

By default, the 100xprompt web app is reachable only from the machine that started it. The **Local access** URL in the startup banner works only on that machine, so your tablet can't open it.

**How to fix it**

1. Stop the server and restart it so it listens for connections from other devices on your network:

   ```bash
   100xprompt web --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096
   ```

2. The startup banner will now show a **Local access** URL plus one or more **Network access** URLs. A network URL looks like `http://192.168.x.x:4096`.

3. On your tablet, open one of the **Network access** URLs. Your tablet needs to be on the same network as the machine running the server.

**Optional: skip looking up the IP address**

If you add `--mdns` to turn on local network discovery, your tablet can reach the app at `http://100xprompt.local:4096` instead.

**Optional: make it the default**

To avoid passing these flags every time, add them to your `100xprompt.json`:

```json
{
  "server": {
    "hostname": "0.0.0.0",
    "port": 4096,
    "mdns": true
  }
}
```

In case it's a concern, your code isn't sent anywhere. The server still runs on your machine and serves your files locally. Opening it to your network only lets your own trusted devices connect to that same server.

If you still have trouble after trying this, reply and we'll be glad to help.

Best regards,
100xprompt Support

Subject: Re: Background subagents returning vague results and causing merge conflicts

Hi there,

Thanks for writing in. All three problems you ran into come from the same setup, so the fix is fairly simple.

**Why this happened**

1. **Vague results and ignored constraints.** Subagents don't share your conversation's memory. Each one starts in its own clean context. Your project constraints were part of your conversation, so they never reached the subagents. A vague brief gets a vague result.

2. **The merge conflict.** Parallel subagents work best on *independent* tasks. When several agents edit the same module at the same time, a merge headache is almost guaranteed. Your subagents were all working on the core user module, so their changes overlapped.

**How to fix your approach**

- **Brief each subagent as if it's starting from nothing.** In every brief, explain what you're trying to do, what's already been ruled out, and exactly what you want reported back. Spell out your project constraints each time. Don't assume a subagent knows them.

- **Only parallelize work that's truly separate.** Don't have several subagents edit the core user module at once. Split the work into tracks that don't touch the same files. For example, one subagent researches the new API, one audits how the module is used today, and one maps the tests. Each reports back a short result, and the edits to the shared module then happen in one place.

- **Use a worktree for risky edits.** A subagent can work in its own git worktree. Its changes stay out of your working tree until you decide to bring them in. If it changes nothing, the workspace cleans itself up. This keeps experimental changes contained so you can review them first.

- **Keep using the background for long jobs.** Running big research or build tasks in the background still makes sense. You get a handle to check status and collect the result when it's done, and you can keep working in the meantime.

For the full details, see our [Background Tasks](/automation/background-tasks) documentation.

If you'd like help splitting up your user-module update into separate tracks, just reply and we'll gladly work through it with you.

Best regards,
100xprompt Support

Hi there,

Thanks for writing in. What you saw is 100xprompt working as designed.

100xprompt doesn't produce an answer in one shot and hope it's right. It works in a loop, the way a careful engineer does: it gathers context, decides on the next concrete step, uses a tool to take that step, checks the result, and repeats until the task is done.

The "check" part of that loop is what you noticed. After every action, 100xprompt reads the outcome. If a command fails, a test breaks, or an edit didn't land as intended, it works out what went wrong and revises its plan instead of pushing ahead. In your session, it:

1. Wrote the file (the import was missing).
2. Ran a test to check its work.
3. Saw the failure and traced it to the missing import.
4. Fixed it in the same session.

Catching small mistakes like a failing test, a typo, or a missing import is a big part of what makes 100xprompt reliable on real work. Handing you code it already knows is broken, or stopping to ask about something it can find and fix itself, would only slow you down.

You're still in control. Reading and searching happen automatically, but edits, new files, and shell commands pause for your approval unless you've given standing permission for those actions. If you'd rather review each step as it happens, you can change what runs freely and what asks in your Permissions settings. For large or ambiguous work, you can also start with a plan-first approach and review the plan before any changes are made.

When the task is actually finished, 100xprompt stops and summarizes what changed, so you can review the result and decide what's next.

If you have any other questions, just reply to this email.

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out, and sorry for the confusion with your new command.

What you're describing sounds like a name clash. If a custom command has the same name as a built-in command, the `/` menu shows only one entry for that name. Your command can end up hidden behind the built-in, so when you pick that entry you get the default action instead of your own.

**How to fix it**

1. **Rename your command file** so it doesn't share a name with any built-in command. Short, memorable names work best (for example, `/triage` rather than `/investigate-a-reported-bug`).
2. **Or namespace it in a subfolder.** A file at `command/release/notes.md` becomes `/release/notes`. This keeps it separate from built-ins and groups related commands together in the menu.

**Make sure the file is in the right place**

100xprompt looks for command files in two locations:

- **Project commands:** `.100xprompt/command/` inside your project. These are shared with everyone working in the repo.
- **Global commands:** `.100xprompt/command/` in your home directory. These are available in every project.

**Check that it shows up**

Once you've renamed it, type `/` to open the menu and start typing your command's name. Fuzzy matching will filter the list as you type. Each entry shows its `description` alongside it, so a clear description makes your command easy to spot and pick out later.

If it still doesn't appear after renaming, reply with the file's name and path and we'll take a closer look.

Best regards,
The 100xprompt Support Team

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out, and sorry the refactor went sideways. From what you describe (fast edits, an unfamiliar codebase, and the agent losing the main thread), a few capabilities are worth adjusting.

**1. Switch to a deep-reasoning model for this task.**
100xprompt lets you choose between frontier models for each task. Fast models are meant for quick edits, and deep-reasoning models are meant for hard problems. A large refactor across dozens of files is a hard problem, so pick a high-reasoning model before you start. The "fast edits" you saw suggest a quick-edit model may have been in use.

**2. Let it learn the codebase before it edits.**
100xprompt can search, navigate, and trace relationships across a whole repository, so its changes are grounded in how your code actually works. Since the codebase is new to you, ask it to explore and map the relevant parts first and make changes only after that.

**3. Break the work into steps and use subagents.**
Multi-step agentic tasks are built for this. The agent can split a big goal into steps and start focused subagents to explore or work in parallel without losing the main thread. Asking for a plan first, and having subagents handle exploration, should keep the overall refactor coherent.

**4. Use persistent memory and context.**
Persistent memory carries facts, decisions, and preferences across sessions, and automatic context management keeps long tasks coherent. We recommend pairing a high-reasoning model with rich project memory for your hardest changes, which is exactly this situation.

**5. Check progress with commands and tests.**
Have the agent run your builds, test suites, and linters as it goes, read the output, and keep iterating until everything passes. Edits are applied precisely and can be reviewed diff by diff, so you can check each step instead of finding problems at the end.

**Suggested approach:** Pick a high-reasoning model, have the agent explore and plan first, run the refactor in steps with subagents, and validate with tests along the way. Once the big change is done, you can switch to a faster model for routine follow-ups.

If you run into trouble after these changes, let us know and we'll dig in further.

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out, and sorry for the confusion. Here's what's happening and how to fix it.

**Why the defaults stopped working**

"Omitted things keep defaults" applies to whole *actions*. Any action you leave out of your `keybinds` keeps its default binding. Once you list an action, though, your value replaces that action's entire default binding. It doesn't add to it.

The default for `app_exit` is `ctrl+c,ctrl+d,<leader>q`. When you set `"app_exit": "ctrl+w"`, you replaced all three of those with just `ctrl+w`.

**The fix: use a comma-separated list**

You can bind several shortcuts to one action by separating them with commas. To keep the defaults and add your new shortcut, include all of them:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://100xprompt.com/config.json",
  "keybinds": {
    "app_exit": "ctrl+c,ctrl+d,<leader>q,ctrl+w"
  }
}
```

After this change, any of `ctrl+c`, `ctrl+d`, `<leader>q` (your leader key, `ctrl+x` by default, then `q`), or `ctrl+w` will exit 100xprompt.

**A couple of tips**

- Use this approach whenever you want to add an alternative shortcut instead of replacing a default: list the default keys alongside your new one.
- If you haven't already, put your `keybinds` in your **global** `100xprompt.json`. That way your custom shortcuts follow you into every project.

Let us know if you run into anything else!

The 100xprompt Support Team

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out. This is expected behavior, and the fix is straightforward.

When you run 100xprompt with `--format json`, the output is **not** a single JSON array. It's a line-delimited stream: 100xprompt emits one JSON object per line as the task progresses. A parser that expects the whole output to be one valid JSON document will fail on it.

**The fix:** parse the output incrementally. Read one line, parse that line, then move to the next, instead of waiting for the whole output to become valid JSON.

Each line is a complete JSON object with a `type`, a `timestamp`, and the `sessionID` it belongs to. For example:

```json
{"type":"step_start","timestamp":1719830400000,"sessionID":"ses_abc123"}
{"type":"tool_use","timestamp":1719830401200,"sessionID":"ses_abc123","part":{"tool":"read","state":{"status":"completed","title":"src/app.ts"}}}
{"type":"text","timestamp":1719830404000,"sessionID":"ses_abc123","part":{"type":"text","text":"Added validation and updated the tests. All 12 tests pass."}}
{"type":"step_finish","timestamp":1719830404100,"sessionID":"ses_abc123"}
```

The event types you'll see are:

- `step_start`: the agent began a new step of work
- `tool_use`: a tool finished running (a file read, an edit, a command, and so on)
- `text`: the agent produced a chunk of its written response
- `step_finish`: a step of work completed
- `error`: something went wrong during the task

If you're using `jq`, it handles line-by-line input naturally. For example, to pull out just the agent's final written answer:

```bash
100xprompt run --format json "Summarize this branch" \
  | jq -r 'select(.type == "text") | .part.text'
```

In your own script, the same approach applies: loop over the output line by line, parse each line as its own JSON object, and filter on `type` for the events you care about. You can do this as the stream arrives, or collect the lines and inspect them at the end.

If you're still running into trouble after switching to line-by-line parsing, just reply with the relevant part of your script and we'll take a look.

uv currently supports only the "subprocess" keyring provider, which invokes the `keyring` command to fetch credentials. To use it, set `--keyring-provider subprocess`, `UV_KEYRING_PROVIDER=subprocess`, or `tool.uv.keyring-provider = "subprocess"`.

Use the `--python` flag. uv lets you request any Python version each time you run a script:

```console
$ uv run --python 3.10 example.py
3.10.15
```

Without the flag, `uv run example.py` uses the default Python version, which may differ from machine to machine. The Python version request documentation has more on how to request versions.

Use the `--lfs` flag. For example:

```console
$ uvx --lfs --from git+https://github.com/astral-sh/lfs-cowsay lfs-cowsay
```

`uv tool install` takes the same flag:

```console
$ uv tool install --lfs git+https://github.com/astral-sh/lfs-cowsay
```

Use the `--no-editable` option:

```console
$ uv sync --no-editable
```

By default, `uv sync` installs the project and other workspace members as editable packages, so changes show up without re-syncing. `--no-editable` turns that off.

Jupyter can be used with uv either **to interact with a project** or **as a standalone tool**.

1. **Within a project:** Run `uv run --with jupyter jupyter lab` to start a Jupyter server with access to the project's virtual environment. Notebooks can then import the project's modules and dependencies. If you need to install packages from within the notebook, the recommended approach is a dedicated kernel. Add `ipykernel` as a dev dependency with `uv add --dev ipykernel`, then create the kernel with `uv run ipython kernel install --user --env VIRTUAL_ENV $(pwd)/.venv --name=project`. Packages installed from the notebook (e.g., `!uv add pydantic` or `!uv pip install pydantic`) then go into the project's virtual environment.

2. **As a standalone tool:** Jupyter can also be used on its own, independent of a project.

Project dependencies go in the `dependencies` list under the `[project]` table of `pyproject.toml`. This table follows the [PEP 621](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/) standard and is what gets used when uploading to PyPI or building a wheel.

Each entry is a string in [dependency specifier](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-specifiers/) syntax. It contains the package name and can optionally include version constraints, extras, or environment markers for platform-specific packages:

```toml title="pyproject.toml"
[project]
name = "albatross"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = [
  # Any version in this range
  "tqdm >=4.66.2,<5",
  # Exactly this version of torch
  "torch ==2.2.2",
  # Install transformers with the torch extra
  "transformers[torch] >=4.39.3,<5",
  # Only install this package on older python versions
  "importlib_metadata >=7.1.0,<8; python_version < '3.10'",
  "mollymawk ==0.1.0"
]
```

### Alternative sources with `tool.uv.sources`

Some patterns, such as editable installs or relative paths, can't be expressed in `project.dependencies`. For these, uv provides the `[tool.uv.sources]` table, which adds alternative sources for use during development. List the package in `dependencies` as usual, then say where it should come from:

```toml title="pyproject.toml"
[project]
name = "example"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["foo"]

[tool.uv.sources]
foo = { path = "./packages/foo" }
```

uv supports these source types:

- **Index**: a package resolved from a specific package index
- **Git**: a Git repository
- **URL**: a remote wheel or source distribution
- **Path**: a local wheel, source distribution, or project directory
- **Workspace**: a member of the current workspace

For example, `uv add torch --index pytorch=https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu` writes both a source entry and an index definition:

```toml title="pyproject.toml"
[project]
dependencies = ["torch"]

[tool.uv.sources]
torch = { index = "pytorch" }

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "pytorch"
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu"
```

An `index` source pins the package to that index, so it won't be downloaded from any other index.

> **Important:** Only uv reads `tool.uv.sources`. Other tools use only the standard `project.dependencies` table. If you also develop with another tool, you'll need to re-specify the source information in that tool's format.

A `requirements.in` file uses the lightweight [requirements file format](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/reference/requirements-file-format/). Put each requirement on its own line:

```requirements title="requirements.in"
httpx
ruff>=0.3.0
```

A requirement can be just a package name, like `httpx`, or it can include a version constraint, like `ruff>=0.3.0`.

The `.in` name is a convention. It separates the file where you declare dependencies from `requirements.txt`, which holds the locked dependencies.

This format does not support optional dependency groups.

Use `uvx` (or its longer form, `uv tool run`) to run a tool in a temporary environment. This works for tools published to Python package indexes, such as `ruff` or `black`.

The error you saw is expected: **unlike `pip`, uv requires a virtual environment by default.** It's a deliberate design choice, not a bug.

**Why uv works this way**

Every Python installation has its own environment, and packages installed there become available to your scripts. It's generally considered best practice not to modify a Python installation's environment directly. This matters most for Python installations that come with your operating system, because the OS often manages those packages itself. Installing into them can interfere with that.

A virtual environment is a lightweight way to keep your project's packages separate from the Python installation's environment. uv defaults to using one so your system Python stays clean.

**How to fix it**

Create a virtual environment first, then install as usual:

```console
$ uv venv
$ uv pip install requests
```

By default, `uv venv` creates the environment in a `.venv` directory. A few other options:

- **Custom name or path:**
  ```console
  $ uv venv my-name
  ```
- **Specific Python version:**
  ```console
  $ uv venv --python 3.11
  ```
  If that Python version isn't already on your system, uv will download it for you.

Once the virtual environment exists, `uv pip install requests` should work as you expect.

Subject: Re: Excluding Windows from `uv lock` resolution

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out. You can tell uv to resolve only for the platforms you target with the `environments` setting.

By default, uv builds a lockfile that covers every platform. If your project supports a narrower set of platforms or Python versions, you can limit resolution by listing PEP 508 environment markers under `environments`. For macOS and Linux only, add this to your `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[tool.uv]
environments = [
    "sys_platform == 'darwin'",
    "sys_platform == 'linux'",
]
```

Then run `uv lock` again. uv will resolve only for macOS and Linux, so the Windows-incompatible dependency should no longer cause the failure.

A related setting you may find useful later is `required-environments`. It works the other way around: instead of narrowing the platforms, it marks a platform the project *must* support. For example, to require Intel macOS:

```toml
[tool.uv]
required-environments = [
    "sys_platform == 'darwin' and platform_machine == 'x86_64'",
]
```

This setting only matters for packages that don't publish a source distribution, such as PyTorch. Those packages can only be installed where the package provides pre-built wheels. If your Linux servers need specific libc support, you can use `minimum-libc-version` together with `required-environments` to choose the libc implementations and minimum versions you support.

For your situation, though, `environments` alone should be enough. The resolution documentation has more detail on both settings, under "Limited resolution environments" and "Required environments."

If you still see resolution errors after adding this, send us the full output of `uv lock` and we'll take a closer look.

Subject: Re: Packages installed with `uv pip install` not persisting with `uv run`

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out. This is expected behavior, and the fix is quick.

**Why your installs aren't sticking**

In a uv project, uv manages a persistent environment in a `.venv` directory next to your `pyproject.toml`. Each time you run `uv run`, uv creates that environment if it doesn't exist, or makes sure it's up to date if it does. "Up to date" means matching your project's declared dependencies. Those live in `pyproject.toml`, and the exact versions are recorded in the `uv.lock` lockfile, which uv creates and updates automatically during `uv run` and `uv sync`.

`uv pip install pandas` changes the environment directly but never adds pandas to your project's dependencies. When `uv run` syncs the environment, pandas isn't part of the project, so your script can't find it. Our documentation advises against modifying the project environment manually with `uv pip install` for this reason.

**The recommended way to add packages**

For packages your project depends on, use `uv add`:

```
uv add pandas
```

This adds pandas to your project's dependencies and installs it into the project environment. After that, `uv run` will keep it there:

```
uv run your_script.py
```

**For one-off needs**

If you only need a package temporarily and don't want it in your project, you have two options:

- `uv run --with <package> ...` adds the package for that single run.
- `uvx` runs command-line tools.

**If you'd rather manage the environment yourself**

If you don't want uv to manage the project environment at all, you can turn off automatic locking and syncing in your `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[tool.uv]
managed = false
```

For most projects, though, `uv add` is the simplest approach. It also keeps your setup reproducible. We recommend committing `uv.lock` to version control so everyone working on the project gets the same package versions. The `.venv` directory doesn't need to be committed, and uv excludes it from git automatically.

Let us know if you run into anything else.

uv Support

Subject: Re: Setting up a workspace with a root project and libraries in `packages/`

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out. A root application with shared libraries under a `packages` directory is the most common workspace layout. uv's documentation describes it as "a root project with a series of accompanying libraries."

**Expected directory layout**

Here's the example from our docs. The workspace has an explicit root at `albatross`, with two libraries (`bird-feeder` and `seeds`) in the `packages` directory:

```text
albatross
├── packages
│   ├── bird-feeder
│   │   ├── pyproject.toml
│   │   └── src
│   │       └── bird_feeder
│   │           ├── __init__.py
│   │           └── foo.py
│   └── seeds
│       ├── pyproject.toml
│       └── src
│           └── seeds
│               ├── __init__.py
│               └── bar.py
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── uv.lock
└── src
    └── albatross
        └── __init__.py
```

Key points:

- **The root is itself a project.** It has its own `pyproject.toml` and source code (`src/albatross`). It counts as a workspace member, alongside the libraries.
- **Each library has its own `pyproject.toml`** and lives under `packages/`.
- **There is one `uv.lock` at the root** for the whole workspace.
- **The root `pyproject.toml` controls membership.** In this example, `seeds` is excluded there. So the workspace has two members: `albatross` (the root) and `bird-feeder`.

If your root project isn't being recognized as a member, check the root `pyproject.toml` first. It should be a complete project definition, and it's where the workspace members and exclusions are declared. If you send us your root `pyproject.toml` and one library's `pyproject.toml`, we can look at the exact configuration with you.

**Things to keep in mind**

- **One Python requirement for all members.** uv takes the intersection of every member's `requires-python` values. If the root and a library declare incompatible ranges, that can cause problems. To test a single member on a Python version the rest of the workspace doesn't support, you may need `uv pip` to install it in a separate virtual environment.
- **Workspaces may not fit every case.** They're not suited to members with conflicting requirements, or members that each need their own virtual environment. In those cases, path dependencies are often a better choice. Each package becomes an independent project, and the root points to the libraries via `tool.uv.sources`:

  ```toml
  [project]
  name = "albatross"
  version = "0.1.0"
  requires-python = ">=3.12"
  dependencies = ["bird-feeder", "tqdm>=4,<5"]

  [tool.uv.sources]
  bird-feeder = { path = "packages/bird-feeder" }

  [build-system]
  requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.5,<0.14"]
  build-backend = "uv_build"
  ```

  This gives you finer control over dependency resolution and virtual environments. The trade-off is that `uv run --package` is no longer available, so you'd run commands from each package's own directory.

For an application with shared internal libraries, the workspace layout above is usually the right fit. Send over your config files and we'll help you find what's tripping up member detection.

uv Support

Subject: Re: Extra packages installed in a new project

Hi,

Thanks for reaching out. What you're seeing is expected. Those extra libraries are dependencies of the package you added.

**Why the extra packages appear**

Most packages need other packages to work. Each package declares these needs as *requirements*: a package name plus a range of acceptable versions. When you add a package to your project, uv has to install everything that package requires so it will actually run. If those requirements have requirements of their own, uv includes those too.

**Direct vs. transitive dependencies**

uv separates the two kinds of dependencies like this:

- **Direct dependencies** are the ones your project defines, i.e., the package you added to your configuration.
- **Indirect (transitive) dependencies** are the ones your direct dependencies bring in. These are the "several other libraries" in your environment.

**How uv chooses versions**

When uv resolves your project, it looks for one set of package versions that satisfies every requirement at once, including the transitive ones. Here's a simple example:

- Your project depends on `foo` and `bar`.
- `foo 1.0.0` requires `lib>=1.0.0`.
- `bar 1.0.0` requires `lib>=2.0.0`.
- `lib` has versions 1.0.0 and 2.0.0.

You never listed `lib` yourself, but both `foo` and `bar` need it, so the resolution has to include it. `foo` accepts either version of `lib`, but `bar` needs 2.0.0 or later, so uv picks `lib 2.0.0`.

Sometimes more than one combination of versions works. In that case the resolver chooses one valid solution that keeps all requirements compatible.

**In short**

Your configuration only lists what you asked for directly. The other installed packages are the transitive dependencies that the package needs in order to work. If you'd like more detail on how requirements are written, the dependency specifiers page in the Python Packaging documentation is a good reference: https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-specifiers/

Let us know if you have any other questions.

Best regards,
uv Support

Hi there,

Replace `<ORGANIZATION>`, `<PROJECT>`, and `<FEED>` with your own values. The two URLs are the same except for the last part: `/simple/` versus `/upload/`.

**2. Supply your access token**

If you're not using keyring, set your credentials as environment variables. The username can be any placeholder value. The token goes in the password:

```console
$ export UV_PUBLISH_USERNAME=dummy
$ export UV_PUBLISH_PASSWORD="$AZURE_ARTIFACTS_TOKEN"
```

```console
$ uv publish --index private-registry
```

```console

```

We recommend the `publish-url` approach, though. With `UV_PUBLISH_URL`, uv can't check whether the package has already been published before it uploads artifacts.

Subject: Re: uv not finding newer PyPI release when using --extra-index-url

Hi,

Thanks for reaching out. What you're seeing is intentional: uv and pip handle packages that exist on more than one index differently.

**Why this happens**

When a package exists on multiple indexes, uv checks the indexes in order, with `--extra-index-url` indexes checked before the default index (PyPI). It stops at the first index that contains the package and only considers the versions available there. Because your internal index has the package, uv never looks at the versions on PyPI, so a version that exists only on PyPI isn't found.

pip combines the candidate versions from all indexes and picks the best one from that combined set. pip doesn't guarantee the order it searches indexes in, and it assumes packages are unique by name and version across all indexes.

**Why uv works this way**

The default protects against "dependency confusion" attacks. In these attacks, someone publishes a malicious package on PyPI with the same name as an internal package, and it gets installed instead of the internal one. The `torchtriton` incident in December 2022 is a well-known example: https://pytorch.org/blog/compromised-nightly-dependency/

If a package exists on your internal index, uv's default is to always install it from there and never from PyPI.

**How to get the behavior you want**

Since v0.1.39, you can change how uv handles multiple indexes with the `--index-strategy` command-line option or the `UV_INDEX_STRATEGY` environment variable:

- `first-index` (default): only consider versions from the first index that contains the package, with `--extra-index-url` indexes checked before the default index.
- `unsafe-first-match`: search all indexes and prefer the first index that has a compatible version.

With `unsafe-first-match`, if your internal index doesn't have a version that meets your requirement, uv can move on and use the newer release from PyPI. In CI, you could set:

```shell
export UV_INDEX_STRATEGY=unsafe-first-match
```

or pass `--index-strategy unsafe-first-match` to your `uv pip install` command.

Please note the "unsafe" in the name. Letting uv fall through to PyPI for a package name you also host internally brings back the dependency confusion risk described above. Before you enable it across your whole pipeline, we'd suggest checking that the package names you host internally are either yours on PyPI too, or that this risk is acceptable for your environment.

If you have any trouble after making this change, send us the command you're running and the resolver output and we'll take a look.

Best regards,
uv Support

Specify project dependencies in the `project.dependencies` table in `pyproject.toml`. It follows PEP 621 and uses dependency specifier syntax. Each entry includes a dependency name and may include version constraints, extras, or environment markers for platform-specific packages. For example:

```toml title="pyproject.toml"
[project]
name = "albatross"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = [
  # Any version in this range
  "tqdm >=4.66.2,<5",
  # Exactly this version of torch
  "torch ==2.2.2",
  # Install transformers with the torch extra
  "transformers[torch] >=4.39.3,<5",
  # Only install this package on older python versions
  # See "Environment Markers" for more information
  "importlib_metadata >=7.1.0,<8; python_version < '3.10'",
  "mollymawk ==0.1.0"
]
```

The `tool.uv.sources` table extends the standard dependency tables with alternative dependency sources, which are used during development. Dependency sources add support for common patterns not supported by `project.dependencies`, like editable installations and relative paths. For example:

```toml title="pyproject.toml"
[project]
name = "example"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["foo"]

[tool.uv.sources]
foo = { path = "./packages/foo" }
```

Sources are only respected by uv. If another tool is used, only the definitions in the standard project tables will be used.

Use a lightweight requirements file format, commonly named `requirements.in`, with each requirement defined on its own line. For example:

The common layout for a root project with accompanying libraries is an explicit root project with libraries under a `packages` directory. For example:

```text
albatross
├── packages
│   ├── bird-feeder
│   │   ├── pyproject.toml
│   │   └── src
│   │       └── bird_feeder
│   │           ├── __init__.py
│   │           └── foo.py
│   └── seeds
│       ├── pyproject.toml
│       └── src
│           └── seeds
│               ├── __init__.py
│               └── bar.py
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── uv.lock
└── src
    └── albatross
        └── __init__.py
```

Here, `albatross` is the explicit root. The workspace has two members total: `albatross` (the root) and `bird-feeder`. `seeds` was excluded in the `pyproject.toml`, so it is not a member. Each package has its own `pyproject.toml` and `src` layout, and the workspace has a single `uv.lock` at the root.

In the root `pyproject.toml`, workspace membership is reflected by including or excluding packages; in the example, excluding `seeds` leaves the root and `bird-feeder` as members. Note that workspaces enforce a single `requires-python` for the entire workspace, taking the intersection of all members’ `requires-python` values. Workspaces are not suited for cases where members have conflicting requirements or desire a separate virtual environment for each member; in those cases, path dependencies are often preferable.

Hi,

Thanks for reaching out. The extra packages are likely transitive dependencies.

In uv’s documentation, dependencies are other packages that are necessary in order for the current package to work. A package defines its dependencies as requirements, roughly a combination of a package name and acceptable versions. The dependencies defined by the current project are called direct dependencies. The dependencies added by each dependency of the current project are called indirect or transitive dependencies.

So, when you explicitly add one package to your configuration, uv treats that as a direct dependency. If that package itself requires other libraries, those are indirect or transitive dependencies. During resolution, uv must find a set of package versions that satisfies the project requirements, and the resolution must also include the transitive dependencies. That is why your environment can contain several other libraries that you never declared directly.

In short: uv distinguishes between what you explicitly requested and what those libraries require by treating your declared packages as direct dependencies and the dependencies added by those packages as indirect or transitive dependencies.

Thanks for reaching out. This is expected behavior. When uv searches for a package across multiple indexes, it iterates over the indexes in order (preferring the `--extra-index-url` over the default index) and stops searching as soon as it finds a match. If a package exists on multiple indexes, uv limits its candidate versions to those present in the first index that contains the package. So if your internal index contains the package, uv will not consider newer versions from PyPI.

This is intentional: uv’s behavior is such that if a package exists on an internal index, it should always be installed from the internal index, and never from PyPI. The intent is to prevent “dependency confusion” attacks.

`pip`, by contrast, combines the candidate versions from all indexes and selects the best version from the combined set, though it makes no guarantees around the order in which it searches indexes.

As of v0.1.39, you can opt in to `pip`-style behavior for multiple indexes via the `--index-strategy` command-line option or the `UV_INDEX_STRATEGY` environment variable. The supported values include `first-index` (default) and `unsafe-first-match`. `first-index` searches for each package across all indexes, limiting candidate versions to those present in the first index that contains the package, prioritizing `--extra-index-url` indexes over the default index URL. `unsafe-first-match` searches for each package across all indexes, but prefers the first index with a compatible version.

You can run commands and scripts in your project environment with `uv run`. For example, to use Flask:

```console
$ uv add flask
$ uv run -- flask run -p 3000
```

Or, to run a script:

```python title="example.py"
# Require a project dependency
import flask

print("hello world")
```

```console
$ uv run example.py
```

Prior to every `uv run` invocation, uv will verify that the lockfile is up-to-date with the `pyproject.toml`, and that the environment is up-to-date with the lockfile, keeping your project in-sync without the need for manual intervention. `uv run` guarantees that your command is run in an environment with all required dependencies at their locked versions.

Note that `uv run` does not remove extraneous packages (those not in the lockfile) from the environment by default.

Alternatively, you can use `uv sync` to manually update the environment, then activate it before executing a command:

macOS and Linux:

```console
$ uv sync
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ flask run -p 3000
$ python example.py
```

Windows:

```pwsh-session
PS> uv sync
PS> .venv\Scripts\activate
PS> flask run -p 3000
PS> python example.py
```

The virtual environment must be active to run scripts and commands in the project without `uv run`. Virtual environment activation differs per shell and platform.

See the documentation on running commands and scripts in projects for more details.

With inline script metadata, add deps via `uv add --script my_notebook.py numpy`, edit with `uvx marimo edit --sandbox my_notebook.py`, and run as a script with `uv run my_notebook.py`. In GitLab CI, set `UV_LINK_MODE=copy` because the build directory is a separate mountpoint. If using a distroless image, specify the entrypoint. Persist the uv cache between runs to improve performance, key it with `uv.lock`, and run `uv cache prune --ci` at the end to reduce cache size. Using `uv pip`? uv requires a virtual environment by default; use `--system` or `UV_SYSTEM_PYTHON` to install into the system environment. See the docs.

Developers: uv now includes **Tools**. Run tools without installing them via `uv tool run`—dependencies go in a temporary virtual environment isolated from your current project. `uvx` is an exact alias for `uv tool run`. You can also install tools with `uv tool install`, making executables available on your `PATH`; an isolated environment is still used and persists until uninstalled. `uvx` environments are cached and disposable—if removed, they’re recreated automatically. Tool environments aren’t intended to be mutated directly. Version behavior is handled too: `uvx` uses the latest version on first invocation, then the cached version unless you request a different version, prune/refresh the cache, or use `@latest`.

uv supports managing PyTorch projects and dependencies across Python versions and environments, including controlling for accelerator choice like CPU-only vs. CUDA. PyTorch wheels often live on dedicated indexes, and builds for different accelerators are published to different indexes (e.g., +cpu and +cu130). Our new guide shows how to configure a PyTorch index in pyproject.toml, use explicit = true so it only applies to PyTorch-related packages, and point torch and torchvision to the desired index with tool.uv.sources. uv now supports creating projects with `uv init`. Choose an application (the default) or a library with `--lib`. Applications are suitable for web servers, scripts, and command-line interfaces. By default, uv defines a build system and places source files in `src/<project_name>/`, enabling packaging features like command-line entry points and avoiding common Python import-system confusion. Use `--no-package` or `--bare` to disable the build system. Create a project in the working directory, or target a name with `uv init foo`; `--directory` changes the working directory. If a `pyproject.toml` already exists, uv exits with an error. Applications include a command definition you can run with `uv run`.

uv now supports preview features for developers. Enable all with `--preview` or `UV_PREVIEW=1`. Enable specific features with `--preview-features foo`, repeat the flag, or use a comma-separated list; `UV_PREVIEW_FEATURES=foo,bar` works similarly. You can also configure `preview-features = ["foo", "bar"]` in `uv.toml`, under `[tool.uv]` in `pyproject.toml`, or in PEP 723 metadata. Set `preview-features = true` to enable all. Some preview features take effect before configuration files are loaded and cannot be enabled from configuration. Often you can use preview features without changing settings when behavior is gated by user interaction—for example, `uv pip install` with a `pylock.toml` file—though a warning is displayed; enabling the feature silences it. Enabling nonexistent preview features warns, but does not error.

The uv team: Build and publish a package with uv. Run `uv build` to build the project in the current directory and place artifacts in `dist/`. You can also build a specified directory with `uv build <SRC>` or a workspace package with `uv build --package <PACKAGE>`. We strongly recommend configuring a build system; projects created with `uv init` include a `[build-system]` by default. When publishing, run `uv build --no-sources` so the package builds correctly when `tool.uv.sources` is disabled, as with other build tools. Use `uv version` to update your package version before publishing—exact versions, `--dry-run`, and `--bump` for components like major, minor, patch, stable, alpha, beta, rc, post, and dev.

Package indexes are here. Define additional indexes in `pyproject.toml` with `[[tool.uv.index]]`: `name` is optional, `url` is required. Indexes are prioritized in the order defined; command-line indexes take precedence. PyPI is the default index by default. To exclude PyPI, set `default = true` on another index or use `--default-index`. The default index is always lowest priority. Pin a package to an index via `tool.uv.sources`; `explicit = true` prevents packages from being installed from that index unless explicitly pinned. Named indexes referenced via `tool.uv.sources` must be defined in the project’s `pyproject.toml`. By default, uv uses `first-index`: it stops at the first index where a package is available, limiting resolutions to that index to help prevent dependency confusion. Opt into other strategies with `--index-strategy` or `UV_INDEX_STRATEGY`.

uv can install packages from JFrog Artifactory using a username and password or a JWT token—add the index to your project in `pyproject.toml`. You can also publish packages by adding a `publish-url` to your index definition.

One JFrog-specific note: using `--token "$JFROG_TOKEN"` or `UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN` will return a 401 Unauthorized error, because JFrog requires an empty username while uv passes `__token__` when `--token` is used. Instead, pass your token as the password with an empty username:

`uv publish --index <index_name> -u "" -p "$JFROG_TOKEN"`

Or set `UV_PUBLISH_USERNAME=""` and `UV_PUBLISH_PASSWORD="$JFROG_TOKEN"`, then run `uv publish --index private-registry`. Note: the publish environment variables do not include the index name.
